justice: Spatial resources are heavily allocated to motor vehicles (multiple wide travel lanes), while no sidewalk or pedestrian space is visible, indicating low equity among road users.

Guardrails on both sides and in the median prioritize high-speed traffic management, but there are no visible provisions for non-motorized users (e.g., crossings, refuge islands, shared-use paths), limiting inclusive access.

Rules appear consistent for drivers (clear lane markings and divided carriageways), but the absence of any visible facilities for walking/cycling suggests the system is not equally enabling for all road users.
No barrier-free features are observable (e.g., curb ramps, accessible crossings, tactile guidance), which reduces accessibility for anyone not in a vehicle.
safety: Median and roadside guardrails provide strong separation between opposing traffic and roadside hazards, reducing head-on and run-off-road crash severity for drivers.
Clear white lane markings and wide lanes improve legibility and lane discipline, supporting safer driving behavior.
The environment appears designed for high speeds (expressway geometry and long sight lines); without visible traffic-calming or crossings, it is inherently unsafe for pedestrians/cyclists if present.
Sparse roadside activity and lack of intersections in view reduce conflict points, which can improve motor-vehicle safety but also reflects limited multimodal safety provisions.
livability: There are no visible destinations or active frontages (no shops, homes, or community facilities), so the corridor offers little support for daily life or social interaction.
No public-space amenities are present (benches, shelters, plazas), limiting opportunities for rest, gathering, or recreation.
The setting is dominated by vehicle infrastructure (multi-lane roadway, guardrails), which reduces perceived human-scale livability for non-driving users.
sustainability: Lack of visible public transport infrastructure (no bus stops, shelters, or stations) suggests limited support for low-carbon mobility choices.
No cycling facilities are visible (no bike lanes, protected paths, or signage), reducing mode shift potential away from cars/trucks.
Some roadside greenery/shrubs are present, offering minor ecological value, but the corridor is largely impervious asphalt with no visible stormwater features (e.g., bioswales).
High-voltage transmission towers and lines indicate energy infrastructure presence, but they do not directly improve transport sustainability in this streetscape.
aesthetics: The roadway is visually orderly (clean asphalt surface, consistent lane markings, continuous guardrails), creating a neat but utilitarian appearance.
Large transmission towers and overhead power lines dominate the skyline and reduce scenic quality.
Green shrubs along the sides add some visual softness, but limited tree canopy and the vast paved surface make the scene feel stark and infrastructure-heavy.
comfort: Thermal comfort is likely low for anyone outside a vehicle because there is no visible shade canopy (few/no street trees over the roadway or along a walkable edge).
Physical comfort for non-motorized users is poor because no sidewalk, shoulder walkway, or resting facilities (benches, pull-offs) are visible.

Psychological comfort for pedestrians/cyclists would be low due to the high-speed expressway character, heavy vehicle presence (truck ahead), and strong barriers that can feel isolating and inhospitable.
For drivers, the smooth pavement and clear markings support a comfortable driving experience with minimal visual clutter at road level.
walkability: No sidewalk or dedicated pedestrian path is visible along either side, making walking functionally unsupported.
Guardrails create a continuous barrier between the roadway and roadside areas, limiting safe pedestrian refuge or recovery space.
No marked crossings, signals, or pedestrian refuges are visible, so route connectivity for walking across or along the corridor is extremely limited.
bikeability: No bike lane markings, protected cycle tracks, or paved shoulder suitable for cycling are visible, indicating very low cycling accommodation.
High-speed traffic geometry and the presence of heavy vehicles (truck) create high stress conditions for cyclists.
Guardrails and narrow edge space reduce escape options and perceived safety for cyclists.
No bicycle-support amenities are visible (bike signage, parking, or wayfinding), reducing cycling convenience and feasibility.
